A stick pusher is designed that way so that the nose can be lowered if the flight crew is somehow incapacitated. It's also to prevent the pilots from doing something stupid like holding back-pressure too long and stalling the aircraft. Overriding usually involves a quick flip of the trim switch on the yoke, and disabling is a matter of pulling a breaker if necessary. This should have been trained on. The stick pusher is for large upsets. The newer 737's also have an MCAS system that will instead use the stabilizer trim to lower the nose if necessary, and it does so much more slowly than a stick pusher would.

"I'm not a pilot, but shouldn't a system that's attempting to detect whether the plane's nose is "too high" actually have an instrument that detects the angle of the plane's nose relative to level? Why would it just assume that slow airspeed means nose down is the best option? Even then, didn't the plane "know" it was on a collision course with terrain? Why did it not correct for that?"

It does. The attitude indicator tells you your pitch and roll angles. But what warns of an impending stall is actually the Angle of Attack indicator, which measures airflow relative to the wing. So it actually has two systems. One tells you your pitch relative to the horizon, and the other relative to the airflow. It wasn't assuming the airspeed was the problem, but that the angle of attack was too high, which is probably why it lowered the nose. AoA is a more reliable indicator, since stall speeds change with altitude and wing configuration, but if the instruments measuring AoA (alpha vanes, one on each side) are malfunctioning, you can have issues. But in the event of a system fuckup like that, there's a defined procedure to, as you pointed out, apply a specific thrust setting and pitch to a specific angle relative to the horizon, where physics dictates you will be travelling at a specific speed (give or take a few knots).

At some point, the plane probably did know it was heading for terrain/water. But by the time the GPWS comes into play, you're at <1,000 feet, and in a severe nose-down attitude, you're not recovering from that. The problem seems to have come from the malfunctioning AoA/MCAS and the erroneous readings not being overridden by the pilots. The system was pitching down because, when a stall is imminent, the corrective procedure is almost always to lower the nose, and trade altitude for airspeed.
